overview: The Union of South Africa joined four former colonies in 1910 as a self-governing British dominion. Its government excluded most Black people from national power, and laws took land, controlled travel and split many working families. Yet people built schools, newspapers, unions, choirs and jazz clubs, and women led powerful protests. The National Party began formal apartheid in 1948; families in Sophiatown faced forced removal, while the 1955 Freedom Charter demanded a different future. Anti-pass protest at Sharpeville ended in police killing in 1960. The Union became a republic in 1961 after a whites-only referendum; the people and their resistance did not end.

periods.title: Union and segregation
periods.summary: A British dominion with a white-minority national government restricted African land, movement and voting rights; people organized against those rules.

periods.title: Apartheid laws and organized resistance
periods.summary: The National Party formalized apartheid through racial classification, spatial removal and unequal schools. Communities resisted through protests, music and the Freedom Charter.

sections.title: Who could rule, live and travel?

items.text: In 1910 four colonies joined as a self-governing British dominion. Black South Africans were excluded from the negotiations. Most people could not vote in national elections, although the Cape had limited nonwhite franchise exceptions. A border on the map never meant everyone inside it had a voice.

The 1913 Land Act barred most African people from buying or renting land outside designated reserves of roughly 7% of the country. It disrupted farming and family livelihoods; the inequality grew with later laws.

White women gained the national vote in 1930. That did not enfranchise Black women, and African men with the limited Cape vote were later removed from the common roll. Voting rights depended harshly on race as well as gender.

After the National Party won power in 1948, apartheid laws classified people by race, separated residential areas and tightened control over Black education and travel. Segregation had existed before 1948; that election was a new legal escalation.

At Sharpeville in 1960, police killed anti-pass protesters. The Union became a republic in 1961 after a referendum from which Black voters were excluded. The name and constitution changed; apartheid continued.

Gold and diamond mines needed workers, but the migrant-labour system often housed men in compounds away from wives, children and fields. A pay packet could travel home more easily than a parent. This was a system of work and separation, not the life of every family.

Charlotte Maxeke, an early Black woman graduate, taught with her husband, wrote about women in isiXhosa, helped organize an anti-pass action in 1913 and founded a women’s league in 1918. Her story connects education, family work and political courage.

The 1953 Bantu Education Act put Black children’s schooling under apartheid control and prepared many for restricted work. Parents and teachers still valued learning and organized for children’s opportunities.

Sophiatown near Johannesburg had a rich social and musical life, including Sunday jazz sessions. In 1955 officials began forcing families out of their homes. A song could remember a neighborhood after a bulldozer erased its street.

In August 1956 about 20,000 women marched to Pretoria against pass laws. Some carried babies; some domestic workers brought children they cared for. The question of who could travel was also a question of who could keep a household together.

The 1955 Freedom Charter said “The people shall govern!” This is an original English-language sample from the resistance movement, not a law the apartheid government followed. The charter also demanded houses, education, health and respect for languages.

sections.title: Health, water and the everyday indignity

items.text: When influenza struck in 1918, Potchefstroom Hospital used tents to care for patients. Its nurses faced enormous pressure. This local hospital account is one window into the pandemic, not a picture of every hospital.

The 1952 pass law required Black South Africans to carry detailed identity and work documents. Getting to a job, relatives or a clinic could involve official permission and the threat of arrest. Women’s anti-pass campaigns insisted that family life could not be separated from movement rights.

A 1953 law separated public amenities by race. A public toilet, beach or waiting room could carry an apartheid sign. Such rules made even ordinary errands an act of enforced inequality; facilities were not equally provided.

ending.text: On 31 May 1961 the Union became the Republic of South Africa after a racially restricted referendum. Formal apartheid, the land crisis and family separations continued under the republic; democracy came only in 1994. The imported map’s 1945 endpoint is a dataset boundary, not the Union’s constitutional end.

sources.title: The Presidency, History of South African Heads of State
sources.note: Union founded 31 May 1910 by negotiation excluding Black South Africans; 31 May 1961 republic followed a racially restricted referendum; 1994 and 1996 constitutional changes.

sources.title: South African History Online, Turning-point Elections 1910–2009
sources.note: Union franchise excluded most people; limited Cape exceptions; white women enfranchised 1930 and African Cape voters removed 1936.

sources.title: South African Parliament, Diagnostic Report on Social Cohesion
sources.note: 1913 Land Act restricted African landownership and renting to roughly 7% designated reserves; 1936 measure and apartheid removals deepened dispossession.

sources.title: South African History Online, Charlotte Maxeke
sources.note: Black woman graduate Charlotte Maxeke taught, wrote in isiXhosa, helped organize 1913 anti-pass action and founded Bantu Women’s League in 1918.

sources.title: South African History Online, Mineral Revolution
sources.note: Gold and diamond work depended on migrant labour, compounds and separation from families, while wealth and risk were distributed unequally.

sources.title: South African History Online, Pass Laws 1800–1994
sources.note: Pass controls preceded 1948; 1952 document law and 1953 Separate Amenities Act restricted Black movement and segregated public facilities.

sources.title: South African History Online, A History of the South African Constitution 1910–1996
sources.note: National Party took power in 1948 and enacted apartheid laws including racial classification, Group Areas and Bantu education.

sources.title: South African History Online, Sophiatown Timeline
sources.note: Forced removal of Sophiatown families began 9 February 1955; first day saw about 150 families moved.

sources.title: South African History Online, The Melody of Freedom
sources.note: Sophiatown jazz clubs and Sunday sessions nurtured musicians; songs commented on removals and bus boycotts.

sources.title: South African History Online, Women’s Resistance Against the Pass Laws
sources.note: Women organized against passes because raids, movement rules and arrests threatened children, homes and wages.

sources.title: South African History Online, The Women’s March Pretoria 1956
sources.note: About 20,000 women marched against passes 9 August 1956; some carried babies or the children they cared for.

sources.title: Nelson Mandela Foundation O’Malley Archives, Freedom Charter 1955
sources.note: Original English document adopted at Kliptown demands popular government, equal language rights, houses, education and health; not apartheid-era law.

sources.title: Potchefstroom Hospital, Our History
sources.note: Local hospital history recalls emergency tents and nursing strain during the 1918 influenza pandemic.

sources.title: South African Embassy, Chronological Points of Reference
sources.note: 1960 Sharpeville massacre followed anti-pass protest; 1961 republic, 1976 Soweto uprising and 1994 democratic transition.

sources.title: South African Government, Milestones of 20 Years of Freedom
sources.note: 27 April 1994 first national nonracial elections gave adults the vote; Mandela inaugurated 10 May; 1996 constitution followed.
